solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Overly-complicated hot boy, perhaps, but not the right hot boy (5,8)

indicatorNotes.but not: tells you to leave out the letters named next

blocks.note: a heartthrob is a boy who is 'hot'
RT is the standard abbreviation for right, removed to leave HEATHROB

annotation.surface: Someone complaining that a dating scene is needlessly tangled.
annotation.walkthrough: The repeated 'hot boy' does two different jobs: first HEARTTHROB, then IN plus SON. William Heath Robinson was a British cartoonist famous for absurdly elaborate contraptions, so his name became an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Heath Robinson describes a machine or plan made ludicrously complicated for a simple job.

entries.clue: Low water measure, a hippo’s been worried (8,3)

indicatorNotes.worried: worried = shaken about, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A hippo fretting as its watering hole dries up.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a hosepipe ban stops people watering gardens or washing cars during a drought; 'low water' is the drought, not a low river.
annotation.definitionFit: A hosepipe ban is the measure water companies impose when reservoirs are low.

entries.clue: Chef might need this for cutting middle of orange (5)

indicatorNotes.cutting: one piece cuts into another, sitting inside it
indicatorNotes.middle of: take the central letters of the next word

blocks.note: the two central letters of orANge

annotation.surface: A kitchen instruction about slicing an orange.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For cutting' reads as a knife's purpose, so a solver hunts for kitchen tools; the two words split apart, one a synonym and one an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Chefs wear aprons to protect their clothes.

entries.clue: Radical had to accept queen — Queen Elizabeth? (9)

indicatorNotes.to accept: to accept is to take in, so HAD takes R inside itself

blocks.note: the Queen Elizabeth is an ocean liner; the question mark flags an example

annotation.surface: A question about whether a monarch was a radical.
annotation.walkthrough: The second Queen is not a monarch at all but the Cunard ship named after one.
annotation.definitionFit: A hardliner holds extreme, uncompromising views, as a radical does.

entries.clue: Wrong composer displacing Bach before church (7)

indicatorNotes.displacing: BACH is pushed out of the composer's name
indicatorNotes.before: before means ahead of in order, so OFFEN is written ahead of CE

blocks.note: Jacques Offenbach, composer of the can-can

annotation.surface: A critic complaining that the wrong composer has replaced Bach in a church concert.
annotation.walkthrough: Bach is not the composer here but part of one, Offenbach.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: wrong as a noun names a misdeed, the same thing an offence is.

entries.clue: Where Rudolph Valentino was regularly cast into a play (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: regularly means at even intervals, so letters are taken at every second step

blocks.note: surface padding: actors are cast into plays
odd letters of I n T o A p L a Y

annotation.surface: The silent-film star being cast in a stage role.
annotation.walkthrough: Valentino, the silent-film heart-throb, was born in Italy; 'cast' only dresses the surface, since actors are cast into plays.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the silent-film star was born and raised in this country before emigrating to America.

entries.clue: Sam, Tim, Rich and Ali each cutting last cutting (9)

indicatorNotes.each cutting last: every name loses its final letter

annotation.surface: A list of four friends and some cutting remark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' appears twice: first as the instruction to trim each name, then as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Satirical remarks are cutting, sharply mocking.

entries.clue: What’s ultimately akin to “neither”? (3)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: take the final letter of each word

annotation.surface: A grammar question about the partner of neither.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: nor is the word that pairs with neither.
annotation.definitionFit: An &lit: read straight, the clue asks which word partners neither, and the last letters of its own words spell that partner.

entries.clue: Pest controller ignoring second customer (4)

blocks.note: a mouser is a cat that catches mice
mo = a moment, a second; removed

annotation.surface: An exterminator overlooking a client.
annotation.walkthrough: The pest controller is a cat, not a person with traps.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anyone who consumes a product or service, paying for it, is a customer in that sense.

entries.clue: Obstinate about plant covering river (10)

indicatorNotes.covering: to cover something is to lie over it, so FACTORY goes around R

blocks.note: a plant is an industrial works

annotation.surface: Someone stubborn about a riverside works.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant' suggests something green; here it is a factory.
annotation.definitionFit: Refractory means stubbornly resistant to control.

entries.clue: Undivided attention’s first lost by foreign correspondent pursuing old article (4-4)

indicatorNotes.lost by: that letter is dropped from what follows
indicatorNotes.pursuing: to pursue is to follow behind, so PENPL follows O

blocks.note: a pen pal abroad writes letters to you

annotation.surface: A news correspondent losing the reader's full attention.
annotation.walkthrough: The foreign correspondent is not a journalist but a friend abroad you exchange letters with. 'Pursuing' is loose: the trimmed pen pal follows only the O, with the article after it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an office or home without internal walls or partitions is described this way.

entries.clue: Ball hosted by Piggy or Kermit (6)

indicatorNotes.hosted by: the answer is held inside the next words

annotation.surface: A Muppets party thrown by Miss Piggy or Kermit.
annotation.walkthrough: A yorker is a cricket delivery pitched right at the batter's feet; 'ball' hints at a dance given by the Muppets.
annotation.definitionFit: In cricket a yorker is a type of ball bowled.

entries.clue: Chrome browser initially worked with each social media environment? (4,7)

indicatorNotes.worked: worked = kneaded into a new shape

annotation.surface: A web browser being tested across every social network.
annotation.walkthrough: Chrome looks like Google's browser, especially next to 'browser'; it is just six letters of fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Social media feeds that only repeat a user's own views are called echo chambers; the question mark flags the figurative sense.

entries.clue: Pope and Saint Augustine finally converted chosen people (10)

indicatorNotes.finally: take the last letter of Augustine
indicatorNotes.converted: the letters are changed into a new form

annotation.surface: A pope and St Augustine converting the chosen people.
annotation.walkthrough: The religious surface makes 'chosen people' look biblical; it just means people appointed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: those picked for a job or office have been appointed to it.

entries.clue: Everybody in West Ham’s applauding during score draw (3,3,3)

blocks.note: a one-all draw is a score draw
a hand is applause; in East London speech the H is dropped, giving 'AND

annotation.surface: All the crowd at West Ham clapping during a drawn football match.
annotation.walkthrough: West Ham is an East London football club, and the Cockney accent of that area drops the H, so 'hand' becomes 'and. A score draw is a draw in which goals were scored, as opposed to 0-0.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the set phrase is an emphatic way of saying every single person, as in a toast or a greeting.

entries.clue: Fancy tea set containing metal material (9)

indicatorNotes.Fancy: fancy = elaborate, so rearrange the letters
indicatorNotes.containing: the rearranged TEA SET holds TIN

annotation.surface: An ornate tea service made from metal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy tea set' reads as fine china; 'fancy' is the instruction to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Satinette is a fabric imitating satin.

entries.clue: Fellow presenter spurning a third salmon (4)

indicatorNotes.spurning: to spurn is to reject, so a third of the word is thrown out

blocks.note: a third of COHOST's six letters, removed

annotation.surface: A TV host turning down a share of a salmon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A third' is a fraction of the word: two letters of six.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is one species of Pacific salmon, also called silver salmon.

entries.clue: Intelligent content of iPad? (4)

indicatorNotes.content of: keep only the inside, dropping the outer letters

blocks.note: an iPad is an example of a tablet, hence the question mark

annotation.surface: A question about what clever material lives on an iPad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like apps or files stored on the device; it means the inner letters of TABLET.
annotation.definitionFit: An able person is capable and clever.

entries.clue: Produce menu, say, put in order, get on well (5-5)

blocks.note: to right something is to put it straight
people who click get on well

annotation.surface: Restaurant advice: write the menu, sort it out, and get along.
annotation.walkthrough: The menu is not a restaurant's but the pop-up list a computer shows when you right-click.
annotation.definitionFit: Right-clicking a mouse produces a context menu, one example of its use.

entries.clue: Greek dish mostly consumed before son writhes (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter goes
indicatorNotes.before: the pieces run in clue order

blocks.note: GYRO, the Greek meat dish, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A son squirming after eating most of a Greek meal.
annotation.walkthrough: A gyro is Greek meat cooked on a vertical spit and served in pitta.
annotation.definitionFit: To writhe is to twist about, as one who gyrates does.

entries.clue: Fruit from “among” spinning as an anagram (6)

indicatorNotes.among: the answer sits among the letters that follow
indicatorNotes.spinning: spinning = turning round, so read it backwards

annotation.surface: A self-referring note about letters being jumbled.
annotation.walkthrough: The word 'anagram' is bait: no letters get shuffled. Ananas is the French and botanical name for pineapple, familiar to crossword solvers.
annotation.definitionFit: Ananas is another name for the pineapple.

entries.clue: Roast which may be on the house (5)

annotation.definition2: which may be on the house

blocks.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly

blocks.clueFragment: which may be on the house
blocks.note: tiles of split stone sit on a roof

annotation.surface: A Sunday roast offered free by the landlord.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the house' pretends to mean free of charge; it means literally on a roof.
annotation.definitionFit: To slate someone is to roast them with criticism, and slates cover roofs.

entries.clue: Doctor getting a round in, lying about being on call, in a roundabout way (4,4)

indicatorNotes.in: in means inside, so A and O are placed within DR
indicatorNotes.lying about: about means turned round, so the whole of DAOR lies the other way
indicatorNotes.being on: being on means attached to, so ROAD is joined on after RING

blocks.note: to ring someone is to call them

annotation.surface: An on-call doctor buying a round of drinks and lying about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A round' is pub drinks in the surface but gives A and O here.
annotation.definitionFit: A ring road circles a town, a roundabout route.

entries.clue: Machine to drag endlessly around (5)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: without an end, so the final letter is cut off
indicatorNotes.around: turn the whole thing back to front

blocks.note: a drag is a BORE, without its final E

annotation.surface: A machine designed to haul things round and round without stopping.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drag' looks like a verb, to pull; it is the noun, a tedious thing.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a programmable device that does work automatically is one kind of machine.

entries.clue: Republican repeatedly engaged in concealing court’s final demand for access (3-1-3-3)

indicatorNotes.repeatedly: AT is used again and again, four times
indicatorNotes.concealing: to conceal is to hide within, so the run of ATs hides T inside it
indicatorNotes.final: take the last letter of court

blocks.note: at = engaged in (at work), four times

annotation.surface: A US politician hiding a court's final ruling.
annotation.walkthrough: The Republican looks like a US politician but is simply R, and the legal words hide a knock at the door.
annotation.definitionFit: Rat-a-tat-tat is the sound of knocking to be let in.

entries.clue: Cycling cheats, what’s left after getting fired? (3)

indicatorNotes.Cycling: move the first letter round to the end

blocks.note: has = cheats, as in 'you've been had'

annotation.surface: Cheats being sacked and what remains of them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fired' pretends to mean sacked from a job; it means burnt, leaving ash.
annotation.definitionFit: Ash is what remains after something is burnt.

entries.clue: Airline using little (4)

annotation.surface: Someone booking a small carrier.
annotation.walkthrough: BA is British Airways, the UK's flag carrier.
annotation.definitionFit: Baby as an adjective means little, as in baby carrots.

entries.clue: Sanctuary opening late with kestrel flying all over the place (6-7)

indicatorNotes.opening late: late = gone, so the first letter is removed
indicatorNotes.flying: the letters fly into a new order

blocks.note: a shelter is a sanctuary; its S is dropped

annotation.surface: A bird sanctuary opening late while a kestrel flaps around.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Late' reads as behind schedule but means dead or former, so the opening letter is gone.
annotation.definitionFit: Helter-skelter means in disorderly haste, all over the place.
